opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction isn't to treat it as cheating in the old sense. The tools are here, and pretending they aren't doesn't help anyone. If a student can hand in a decent essay that an AI wrote, that tells me something about the assignment as much as about the student. A lot of homework was designed for a world where producing the text was the hard part. Now producing text is cheap, so we have to ask what we were actually trying to teach.

What I tell students is roughly this: you can use AI, but you have to own the result. If you submit something, you should be able to explain every argument in it, defend it, and say where you disagree with what the model gave you. If you can't, then you haven't really done the work. You've just passed something along. That's a problem not because of some rule, but because you've skipped the part where you actually get better.

On the teaching side, I think we need to shift toward things that are harder to outsource: in-class discussion, oral explanations, iterative projects where we see how your thinking developed, and assignments that ask you to critique or improve on an AI's answer rather than produce one from scratch. Some of my most interesting submissions now are students saying, "Here's what the model said, here's where it's wrong, and here's why."

So I don't see it as purely bad. It raises the bar. The baseline of what anyone can produce has gone up, and the question becomes what you add on top of that. The students who use AI to think more, not less, are going to be in a very good position. The ones who use it to avoid thinking are mostly cheating themselves.

r002.rationale: It says students who use AI to avoid thinking are cheating themselves, but does not state that overreliance fails to help them in final exams.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was anger, and my second reaction was that the anger was misplaced. If a student can hand me an AI-written essay and I can't tell the difference, that says more about the assignment than about the student. I was asking for something a machine can produce in thirty seconds, and then I was surprised when a seventeen-year-old took the shortcut.

So at our school we tried to separate two questions. One is cheating, and that's still cheating. If I say "write this yourself" and you don't, that's a trust problem, and we treat it as one. But the bigger question is what the homework was actually for. A lot of it was never really about the essay. It was about forcing the student to sit with an idea long enough to form an opinion. The essay was just evidence that the thinking happened.

Once you see it that way, the fix isn't detection software. Detection is an arms race we will lose, and it poisons the relationship because you start treating every kid as a suspect. What we did instead was move more of the thinking into the room. Students draft with AI if they want, but then they have to defend it out loud, or revise it against a critique, or explain why they rejected what the model suggested. The ones who outsourced everything fall apart in about two minutes. The ones who used it as a sparring partner are often better than they were before.

I won't pretend it's solved. Some teachers feel like the ground shifted under them, and they're right. But I keep coming back to this: our job was never to collect homework. It was to make sure something happened inside the student's head. If AI forces us to actually check for that instead of trusting a stack of paper, that's uncomfortable, but it's probably overdue.

r002.rationale: It says students who outsourced their thinking struggle to defend it, but does not state that AI overreliance fails to help on final exams.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between using AI to help you learn and using it to avoid learning. If a student asks AI to explain a concept, then works through the problem themselves, that can be useful. But submitting an AI-written answer as your own makes it difficult for a teacher to know what you actually understand.

At our school, I’d want clear expectations for each assignment: whether AI is allowed, how students should disclose its use, and what they need to demonstrate independently. I’d also put more emphasis on the process—drafts, reasoning, and being able to explain your answer. The question is whether students are developing their own judgment.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between using AI to support learning and using it to replace the work of learning. If a student submits an AI-written assignment as their own, we can’t tell what they actually understand. That’s a problem for both assessment and academic honesty.

But I wouldn’t assume every use of AI is cheating. Asking it to explain a concept or give feedback on a draft can be useful, provided the assignment allows it and the student acknowledges that help. Schools need clear expectations, and teachers need opportunities to hear students explain their reasoning. The central question is: can the student understand, defend, and apply what they’ve submitted?
